h: Beach huts, Spartans and seaside history
p: Blyth has a real working-town character, built on its port, coal and shipbuilding past, and it's still a busy harbour today. Out to sea you'll often spot wind turbines on the horizon, part of the town's newer role in renewable energy. It's an honest, down-to-earth place, and that suits a good old market morning perfectly.

Once you've filled your bag, head down to the beach. Blyth's long sandy stretch is lined with colourful beach huts along the promenade, which make a cheerful backdrop for a photo and a flask of tea. Ridley Park, close to the centre, is a pleasant green space with play areas, so it's handy if the kids need to burn off some energy after an hour of rummaging.

Football fans will know the name Blyth Spartans, the non-league club famous for a giant-killing FA Cup run in 1978 that took them all the way to the quarter-finals. Their ground, Croft Park, is close to the town centre, and local matches are a cheap and friendly afternoon out.

For a bigger day, Seaton Delaval Hall, a grand National Trust house designed by Sir John Vanbrugh, is just a short drive south. Keep going along the coast and you'll reach Whitley Bay and St Mary's Lighthouse, reached by a causeway at low tide. Check the tide times before setting off across, as the path disappears under the sea when the water comes in.
